# zipstream: make a telemetry codec stream, in a fifth of the memory a frame needs

## What the task is

### Objective

`3684 / 20000 chars`

`/app` holds `zipstream`, the lossless codec a fleet telemetry agent uses to
ship log and metric streams to a collector. It works — every stream it writes
reads back byte for byte and the visible suite passes — and it is the wrong
shape for the device it runs on. It reads the whole stream into memory before
it can emit a byte, because it builds one order-0 Huffman table from
statistics of the entire payload; it writes that 256-byte table into the head
of every frame, so a 200-byte record costs 372 bytes to send; and it models
nothing beyond how often each byte value occurs.

Replace it with a codec that streams. Same package, same public API, same
guarantees. Four requirements hold at once, and each of them rules out the
cheap way of getting the others.

1. **The stream protocol (§2).** `source` has exactly one method, `read(n)`
   with `n > 0`. There is no `read()`, no `seek`, no `tell`, no length: the
   size of the stream is not knowable until it ends, and a short read does
   not mean end of stream. `sink` has exactly one method, `write(b)` — you
   cannot rewind to patch a header you already wrote. So there is no second
   pass, and no way to emit a table computed from a payload the far end has
   not seen yet. On top of that, the frame must be a function of the input
   bytes alone: the same payload delivered in different chunk sizes must
   produce a byte-identical frame, and at least 25% of the frame must already
   have been written by the time the source first returns `b""`.

2. **The memory budget (§4).** Each call runs in a fresh interpreter with
   `tracemalloc` started before the package is imported. The traced bytes
   alive when the entry point is called must stay under 384 KiB, and the peak
   during the call, above that baseline, must also stay under 384 KiB. Graded
   streams are 512 KiB and 896 KiB, so neither buffering the stream during
   the call nor pre-allocating a buffer at import time fits. The working set
   must also be independent of stream length: the figure on the 896 KiB
   stream may exceed the one on the 512 KiB stream by at most 32 KiB.

3. **The compression targets (§5).** Five 512 KiB profiles — logfmt lines,
   CSV metric rows, JSON lines, a binary record format of varints and IEEE
   doubles, and a five-segment mixture — each carry a target expressed as a
   fraction of what the shipping v1 codec produces on the same bytes, which
   the grader computes itself: 0.52, 0.56, 0.50, 0.92 and 0.65. Missing a
   target earns credit interpolated from the shipping codec's own size, so
   progress always counts.

4. **The ceilings (§6).** Graded as hard as the targets, because the cheap
   way to hit a ratio is a model that collapses everywhere else.
   Incompressible input must expand by no more than `n/64 + 64` bytes;
   base64 payload lines, which carry six bits in every eight-bit byte, must
   not exceed 1.04× the shipping codec; 512 KiB of one repeated byte must
   compress to under `n/100`, which is eight times below the one-bit-per-
   symbol floor a pure Huffman coder cannot cross; and a stream cycling
   through all 256 byte values must reach `n/10`. §7 adds the complement:
   compressing two differently-shaped halves as one stream must cost no more
   than 1.05× compressing them apart, so a model that stops learning fails.

Done means: `tests/test.sh` exits 0. Standard library only; `zlib`, `gzip`,
`bz2`, `lzma` and every equivalent are unimportable in the grading process,
along with `ctypes`, `subprocess`, `socket` and `tracemalloc`. Every file you
add lives inside `/app/zipstream/`, and the package is at most 96 KiB of
Python. Nothing in the grade is a wall-clock measurement.

### Motivation

`1284 / 10000 chars`

Every fleet agent that ships logs or metrics off a device hits this exact
wall, and hits it in this exact order. Version one compresses a buffer,
because a buffer is what the API gives you. Then the streams get longer than
the device's spare memory, the collector starts counting egress bytes, and
somebody notices that most of what is being sent is the same twenty field
names over and over. The rewrite that follows is not "add compression" — the
compression is already there — it is the considerably harder job of keeping
the ratio while giving up the two things that made it easy: seeing the whole
payload, and having somewhere to put it.

That is the shape of a real optimisation task and it is why the constraints
here are not independent. Backward-adaptive modelling, where both ends
rebuild the same tables from data they have already processed, exists
precisely because you cannot transmit a table you computed from bytes the
decoder has not received yet. Deflate's stored-block escape exists because an
entropy coder inflates random data. Bounded windows exist because the device
has 256 KiB, not 32 MB. An engineer who has built one of these recognises
every requirement in the specification; an engineer who has not will discover
them in the order the grader reports them.

## Difficulty & effort

### Difficulty explanation

`3368 / 20000 chars`

The difficulty is not that any one requirement is hard. It is that the
obvious way to satisfy each one is ruled out by another, so a submission has
to be designed rather than assembled, and the design has to be chosen before
much of the code is written.

**The trap that costs the most is the two-pass reflex.** Every textbook
Huffman coder counts symbols, builds a table, writes the table, then writes
the payload. That is what `/app` does. The natural fix — read in blocks and
emit a table per block — is *worse* on small frames and still needs a
seekable sink for the header on large ones. The way out is backward-adaptive
coding: both ends derive identical tables from statistics of data they have
already handled, so no table is ever transmitted. That idea is not hinted at
anywhere in the specification, and a submission that does not find it cannot
simultaneously reach the ratio targets and the framing bound.

**The second trap is that the constraints are only jointly satisfiable in a
narrow band.** LZ77 with a large window gets the text profiles easily and
fails the memory budget; an order-1 byte model with 256 contexts is 128 KiB
of counters before any code tables exist, and materialising 256 canonical
code tables in Python is megabytes. Something has to give, and working out
*what* — a smaller window, hashed or bucketed contexts, fixed-size arrays
instead of dicts, tables rewritten in place instead of rebuilt — is the
engineering. The reference solution rebuilds its five code tables in place
on every block specifically because allocating new ones keeps two full sets
alive at hand-over, and on this budget that alone is most of the allowance.

**The third trap is that ratio and ceiling pull in opposite directions.**
A pure LZ codec expands base64 and fails §6. An entropy coder with no escape
inflates random data and fails the expansion bound. A pure Huffman coder
cannot spend under one bit per symbol, so the repeated-byte ceiling
(`n/100`, eight times below that floor) is unreachable without matches, run
coding, or arithmetic coding. Each of those is a *different* mechanism, and
the ceilings are chosen so no single one covers all of them.

**The fourth is subtle and will be discovered by failing.** Short reads.
`while chunk := source.read(N)` looks correct and is not: the graded source
returns fewer bytes than asked for on part of its schedule, so a codec that
blocks on read boundaries produces a different frame under a different read
schedule, and §2.3 compares the two frames byte for byte. The same class of
bug hides at the other end: zero padding invented past the end of a
truncated frame is indistinguishable from a real end-of-frame tag unless the
reader tracks which bits were real. The reference had exactly that bug, and
the suite caught it.

It is achievable, and the shape of the answer is standard. A competent
engineer who has written an entropy coder before will recognise the target
as roughly deflate-class and get there: the reference is LZ77 over an 8 KiB
window plus a backward-adaptive contextual Huffman model, 29 KiB of
Python, and it clears every target with 20–25% margin on the text profiles.
The work is in the joint design, the memory accounting, and the two or three
bugs that only appear at a block boundary — which is why seven hours is
honest and why a frontier model is unlikely to one-shot it.

### Expert time estimate (hours)

7

## Oracle & verification

### Oracle strategy

`2756 / 20000 chars`

`solution/reference/zipstream/` is a complete v2 codec, 29 KiB of pure
standard-library Python in eight modules, and `solution/solve.sh` copies it
over `/app/zipstream` and then smoke-tests it before the verifier ever runs.

It is LZ77 over a bounded window, entropy-coded with a backward-adaptive
contextual Huffman model:

* **The frame** is a sequence of byte-aligned blocks: a two-byte `ZS` magic,
  then per block a tag byte (end / compressed / stored) and a two-byte
  payload length, then either a bit-packed symbol stream padded to a byte
  boundary or the raw bytes. Three bytes of overhead per 8 KiB block, and
  three bytes for an empty stream.
* **No code table is ever written down.** Both ends rebuild the same five
  tables at the same points in the symbol stream, from the statistics of the
  blocks they have already handled. Two rules keep them in lockstep: counts
  are rescaled only at block boundaries, never mid-block, so it does not
  matter that the encoder applies a block's counts in one go while the
  decoder applies them one symbol at a time; and a stored block still
  updates the literal statistics from its raw bytes, which both ends can see.
* **The model** is one alphabet of 256 literals plus 29 length codes, split
  across four contexts selected by the top two bits of the previous byte,
  plus a 26-symbol distance alphabet. Four contexts capture most of the
  first-order structure in telemetry without dividing the statistics too
  finely to converge — and without the 256 sparse tables that would not fit
  the budget.
* **The matcher** is a 8 KiB window with a 8192-entry hash head and an
  8192-entry chain, all `array("i")` allocated once. The window size is the
  knob that trades ratio against the budget: 8 KiB costs about one percent
  against 32 KiB on telemetry and leaves room for the model.
* **Stored blocks** handle incompressible input: a block whose coded form is
  no smaller than its input is emitted raw, so random data costs three bytes
  per 8 KiB rather than the 6% an entropy coder would add.

Measured through the real `tests/test.sh` entrypoint at seed 20260818:
**1.0000, PASS**, every one of the 38 checks in all nine categories, 48 codec

Ratios 0.2466 (logfmt), 0.2535 (csv), 0.2120 (jsonl), 0.7928 (binlog), 0.4776
(mixed); as fractions of the shipping codec that is 0.377, 0.424, 0.346,

### Verification strategy

`3551 / 20000 chars`

**The visible half** is `/app/public_tests/test_public.py` — 23 tests that
pass on the untouched seed and describe only what must not regress: the API
exists, the exception hierarchy holds, everything round-trips including
empty and binary payloads, short reads do not truncate, frames start with
`ZS`, and damaged input raises `CorruptStream`. Not one of them looks at
memory, ratio, or streaming. The instructions say so in as many words. The
grader re-runs its **own pristine copy**, so editing the local one changes
nothing.

**The hidden half** is all of `tests/`: the grader, the stream harness, the
corpus generator and the sealed baseline. 38 checks across nine categories,
every graded stream synthesised at grading time from the run seed.

| category | weight | checks | what it grades |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| contract | 0.13 | 5 | short reads, chunk-invariance, output before EOF, no forbidden attribute access |
| roundtrip | 0.19 | 10 | exact recovery of six profiles plus random, repeated, cycling and a nine-segment heterogeneous stream |
| memory | 0.13 | 4 | working set both directions, import footprint, and independence from stream length |
| framing | 0.09 | 3 | seven small frames in aggregate, and two small compressible payloads |
| ratio | 0.26 | 5 | the metric, continuous, against the sealed baseline on the same bytes |
| ceiling | 0.09 | 4 | expansion, six-bit payloads, one repeated byte, a byte cycle |
| adaptivity | 0.06 | 2 | joined vs separate, in both orders |
| robustness | 0.05 | 4 | its own frames truncated at 30%, 60%, 95% and one byte short |
| regression | 0.00 | 1 | the visible suite; its pass ratio multiplies the score |

Four structural decisions do most of the work, and each is a property of the
harness rather than a test somebody remembered to write.

* **Compression and decompression never share a process.** Nothing but the
  frame on disk crosses between them, which makes "stash the payload in a
  global and return a receipt" impossible rather than forbidden. Verified: a
  submission that does exactly that scores 0.
* **The source and the sink have one method each.** `seek`, `tell`,
  `getvalue`, `__len__` and everything else raise, and the attempt is
  recorded. `read()` with no size raises too. The length of the stream is
  genuinely unavailable, so a two-pass design cannot be written, not merely
  cannot be justified.
* **Only `zipstream/**.py` is copied into a tree the grader owns**, and the
  run happens there — which kills `conftest.py`, `sitecustomize.py`,
  `pytest.ini` and edits to the visible suite in one move. The collected
  source is then tokenised, so a docstring that says "unlike zlib, this
  models the data itself" is clean while `import zlib` is not. Both
  directions verified.
* **The memory budget is a precondition for every other measurement.** A
  call that exceeds it yields no usable result, so the checks that depend on
  it score zero — including round-trip. That is deliberate and it is stated
  in the instructions: the code in `/app` already round-trips correctly, and
  crediting correctness would be crediting the starting workspace.

Targets are self-calibrating. Every ratio bound is a fraction of what the
**shipping v1 codec** produces on the same generated stream, computed by the
grader from the byte histogram and the same Huffman construction. An absolute
ratio would drift with the seed; measuring both codecs on the same bytes
cancels the drift — the reference's fraction moves by under 1% across two
dozen seeds on every profile.

## Scoring & exploits

### Binary success condition

`537 / 10000 chars`

`tests/test.sh` exits 0, which happens exactly when the weighted score
written to `/logs/reward.txt` reaches `[verifier] pass_threshold` = **0.88**
and no integrity violation was found. Equivalently: the codec round-trips
every graded stream exactly while holding both memory budgets, produces a
byte-identical frame however the source chunks its reads, meets the five
compression targets and the four ceilings, keeps adapting across a change of
profile, reports truncated frames as `CorruptStream`, and does not break the
visible suite.

### Partial score strategy

`1807 / 10000 chars`

Continuous and monotone. Eight scored categories with the weights in the
table above, summing to 1.00; the ninth, `regression`, has weight zero and
its pass ratio **multiplies** the total, so keeping the visible suite green
earns nothing and breaking it costs proportionally rather than off a cliff.
A category's score is its earned points over its possible points, and a
category whose measurements could not run contributes zero to the numerator
and its full weight to the denominator — an unrunnable check is never a free
pass.

The `ratio` category is the continuous one. Each of the five streams scores
`(baseline - achieved) / (baseline - target)`, clamped to `[0, 1]`, where
`baseline` is the shipping codec's output on the same bytes. Reaching the
target is full marks; matching the shipping codec is zero; anything between
is credited in proportion. An integrity violation — a forbidden name in the
source, or a package over 96 KiB — zeroes the whole score regardless of
behaviour.

Measured landing points, all through the real entrypoint:

| submission | score | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the reference | **1.0000** | — |
| streams correctly, models nothing (LZ disabled, four-context Huffman) | **0.7332** | ratio 42.6%, framing 33%, ceiling 50% |
| keeps the payload in a module global | **0.0000** | decompression is a different process |
| writes the payload to a side file | **0.0000** | the audit hook denies the write |
| the untouched starting workspace | **0.0000** | every category |

The wrong-but-plausible variant is the one worth reading: it satisfies the
stream protocol, the memory budget, adaptivity and robustness in full, and
still fails, because doing the streaming work without doing the modelling
work leaves it 0.15 below the threshold. That is the gap the task is about.

### Anticipated exploits

`5573 / 20000 chars`

**Keep the payload and hand back a receipt.** The oldest trick in compression
benchmarking: `compress` stores the bytes in a module global, a class
attribute or a file, and `decompress` reads them back. *Countermeasure:*
structural. Compression and decompression run in **different processes** and
the only thing that crosses is the frame on disk, so a global does not
survive. An audit hook denies every filesystem write, socket and subprocess
for the duration of a call, and the child's working directory is checked for
new files afterwards. Both variants were built and graded: **0.0000**.

**Call a compression library.** `zlib.compress` is a one-line win over every
ratio target. *Countermeasure:* two layers. At runtime a meta-path finder
makes `zlib`, `gzip`, `bz2`, `lzma`, `zipfile`, `tarfile`, `brotli`,
`zstandard`, `lz4`, `snappy`, `ctypes`, `subprocess`, `multiprocessing`,
`socket` and `tracemalloc` unimportable *before* the submission is imported,
and they are removed from `sys.modules` first so a cached entry does not slip
through. Verified against the direct import, the `importlib` route and
`codecs.encode(data, "zlib_codec")` — the last one names no forbidden module
at all, and is blocked because the codec registry has to import `zlib` to
serve it. Statically, the tokenised scan rejects the names outright.

**Turn off the instrument.** `tracemalloc.stop()` inside the codec would make
any working set reportable. *Countermeasure:* `tracemalloc` is on the blocked
list and in the scan, and the child re-checks `tracemalloc.is_tracing()`
after every call and records a violation if it is not.

**Slurp anyway, quietly.** Read the whole stream but allocate the buffer at
import time so the working set looks flat. *Countermeasure:* the import
footprint is measured and bounded at 384 KiB, and graded streams are 512 KiB
and 896 KiB, so no buffer that could hold one fits under either figure. The
working set is also required to be independent of stream length, which a
partial buffering strategy cannot fake.

**Buffer the output instead of the input.** Compress into memory and write
the frame in one call at the end, dodging the non-seekable sink.
*Countermeasure:* the sink records how much output existed at the moment the
source first returned `b""`; at least 25% must be there. The working-set
bound catches the large cases and this catches the rest — including the
version that writes a header up front to look incremental, because the
measurement is of bytes delivered, not of the first call.

**Overfit the visible corpus.** `/app/samples/` ships five real streams; a
frequency table or dictionary trained on them, baked into the source, is a
legitimate technique and a tempting shortcut. *Countermeasure:* graded
streams are generated at grading time with a **fresh vocabulary** — host
names, service names, field names, message words, series identifiers and
record field order all drawn per run — so a table fitted to the samples
transfers much less well than it appears to. The 96 KiB source cap bounds how
much dictionary can be shipped, and any dictionary loaded into memory
competes with the model for the same 384 KiB. A modest win from a baked-in
skeleton is real, and left legitimate: it is what a zstd dictionary is, and
it does not substitute for adaptive modelling.

**Overfit the visible tests.** *Countermeasure:* the visible suite describes
only what must not regress, is scored at weight zero, and the grader runs its
own pristine copy from `tests/public_reference/`, so a local edit changes
nothing. The instructions say the visible tests are the floor, not the target.

**Interfere with the runner.** `conftest.py` that patches assertions,
`sitecustomize.py` that runs at interpreter start, `pytest.ini` that
deselects, an edited visible suite. *Countermeasure:* structural — only
`zipstream/**.py` is collected into a tree the grader owns and the runs
happen there, so none of those files exists at grading time; a `conftest.py`
*inside* the package is dropped by name.

**Detect the grader and behave differently.** `PYTEST_CURRENT_TEST`,
`sys.argv`, `sys.modules`, `os.environ`, `inspect.stack`, `sys._getframe`.
*Countermeasure:* the tokenised scan looks at `NAME` tokens and at string
literals, so it sees `sys.modules` and the `PYTEST_CURRENT_TEST` literal but
not a docstring that mentions them; an integrity finding zeroes the score.
The spec forbids all of it in §10, so a legitimate submission is never
surprised by the defence.

**Win the metric and lose the point.** Reach the ratio targets with a model
that inflates random data, expands base64, or cannot beat one bit per symbol
on a constant stream. *Countermeasure:* the four ceilings in §6, each aimed
at a different mechanism, plus the adaptivity check in §7 — and the ceilings
are worth 0.15 between them, so they cannot be traded away for ratio.

**Pass by not finishing.** An infinite loop or a hang produces no report.
*Countermeasure:* each codec call is capped at 120 s in its own subprocess
and the whole run holds a 780 s deadline; a call that times out or is never
reached scores zero for every check that depends on it, and the report still
prints. The reference averages 1.8 s per call.

**Leave a reward file behind.** The agent can write to `/logs`; a
`reward.txt` containing `1.0` left there before the verifier runs would be
indistinguishable from a perfect score. *Countermeasure:* the grader deletes
every stale reward artefact from every candidate directory before it does
anything else, then publishes a 0.0 floor, then the real score.

* Reference: 29,088 bytes of Python in 8 modules, against a 98,304 cap.
  Working set 238,732 B compress / 155,864 B decompress against a 393,216 B
  budget; import footprint 142,940 B; working-set drift between a 512 KiB and
  an 896 KiB stream, 144 B against an allowed 32,768.
* Ratio stability across 14 seeds at 512 KiB, as a fraction of the sealed
  baseline: logfmt 0.384–0.405, csv 0.410–0.448, jsonl 0.345–0.378, binlog
  0.863–0.870, mixed 0.568–0.575, opaque 1.0076–1.0077. Targets sit 20–25%
  above the reference on the text profiles, 5% on binlog, 12% on mixed.
* `_corpus._mixed` deliberately uses a FIXED segment plan and varies only the
  vocabulary. The first version shuffled the profile order too, and the
  reference's fraction of baseline then ranged 0.506–0.681 across seeds,
  which would have made the mixed target a lottery.

Three bugs the suite caught, all in the reference:

* **A frame truncated by exactly one byte was accepted as complete.** The bit
  reader invents zero padding past the end of the source so the last symbol
  can be peeked; that padded `0x00` is indistinguishable from the
  end-of-frame tag. The reference passed `robustness.last_byte_gone` by luck
  of bit alignment and the LZ-disabled variant failed it, which is what
  exposed it. `BitReader` now tracks how many bits in the accumulator came
  from the source, and the structural reads refuse to be served invented
  bytes. Re-verified over 442 truncation points: all detected.
* **An index overrun in the match finder** when a candidate match reached the
  end of the available window — `data[other + best_length]` past the end of
  the comparison slice. Found on the first run against real data.
* **Rebuilding code tables by allocation** kept two full sets of five tables
  alive at hand-over and cost ~35 KiB of the budget. Tables are now rewritten
  in place.

Things that could not be verified in this session, and are marked as such
rather than implied:

* **The image has not been built.** There is no docker daemon on the
  authoring host. `environment/selfcheck.py` — the build-time assertion that
  the seed works *and* is still inadequate — was run directly against the
  starter and passes; the visible suite was run directly and passes 23/23.
  Build the image once before submitting.
* **`taskset` does not exist here** (Windows), so the `cpus = 1` claim was
  checked by starvation rather than by pinning: the full suite was re-run
  under 32 competing busy loops on 16 cores -- roughly a third of a core --
  and still scored **1.0000**, in 447 s wall against the grader's 780 s
  deadline. The verifier runs one child process at a time and never threads,
  so it is a single-core workload by construction; on a dedicated core it
  takes about 90 s.
* `[verifier] timeout_sec = 1000` against a 1200 s form default, and the
  grader's own deadline is 780 s. The reference needs 90 s, so the margin is
  about 8x; a submission an order of magnitude slower than the reference
  still finishes.
